question: Why is my period 5 days late
alternate_questions: Should I worry about 5 day delay
answer: A 5-day delay can be caused by stress, illness, travel, weight changes, intense exercise, or pregnancy. If you've had unprotected sex, take a pregnancy test. If not, consider recent lifestyle changes. A single late period is usually not concerning, but if delays become frequent or you have other symptoms like severe pain or unusual discharge, consult a healthcare provider.

question: Why is my period 10 days late
alternate_questions: Should I worry about 10 day delay
answer: A 10-day delay warrants attention. If pregnancy is possible, take a test immediately. If negative and you have no other symptoms, wait a few more days and retest. Common non-pregnancy causes include significant stress, recent illness, travel across time zones, starting or stopping birth control, weight changes, PCOS, thyroid issues, or perimenopause. If your period doesn't arrive within 2 weeks or you have concerning symptoms, see a doctor.

question: Why is my period 2 weeks late
answer: A 2-week delay is significant. Take a pregnancy test if there's any possibility of pregnancy. If negative, consider: recent stress or trauma, significant weight loss or gain, excessive exercise, illness, medication changes, thyroid problems, PCOS, elevated prolactin, or perimenopause. If you're not pregnant and your period hasn't arrived, schedule a healthcare appointment. They may do blood tests, ultrasound, or hormone panels.

question: Can stress delay my period
alternate_questions: Can worry make me miss my period
answer: Yes, significant stress can absolutely delay or even stop your period. Stress increases cortisol, which can interfere with the hypothalamus-pituitary-ovary axis that regulates your cycle. Acute stress (exams, work deadline, breakup) might delay by a few days. Chronic stress can cause longer delays. Managing stress through exercise, meditation, therapy, or lifestyle changes usually helps your cycle return to normal.

question: Can travel delay my period
alternate_questions: Why did my period come late after vacation
answer: Yes, travel can delay your period. Crossing time zones disrupts your circadian rhythm, which affects hormone production. Jet lag, changes in sleep patterns, dehydration from flying, and travel stress can all contribute. The delay is usually temporary, and your cycle should normalize within a month or two after returning home. Stay hydrated, try to adjust to local time quickly, and maintain healthy habits while traveling.

question: Can weight loss delay my period
alternate_questions: Why did my period stop when I lost weight
answer: Yes, significant weight loss can delay or stop your period. Your body needs adequate fat stores to produce estrogen. Losing more than 10% of your body weight quickly, being underweight (BMI under 18.5), or having very low body fat can cause hypothalamic amenorrhea. This is your body's way of conserving energy when it thinks food is scarce. Gradual, healthy weight loss and adequate nutrition help maintain regular cycles.

question: Can weight gain delay my period
alternate_questions: Why did my period change when I gained weight
answer: Yes, significant weight gain can delay or disrupt your period. Excess body fat increases estrogen production, which can disrupt the normal hormonal balance. Obesity is associated with irregular cycles, heavier periods, and conditions like PCOS. Losing even 5-10% of body weight can help regulate cycles. If weight gain is sudden or unexplained, consult a healthcare provider to rule out thyroid issues or other conditions.

question: Can exercise delay my period
alternate_questions: Why did my period stop with exercise
answer: Yes, excessive exercise can delay or stop your period. This is called exercise-induced amenorrhea and is common in elite athletes or those with very intense training regimens. It happens because your body redirects energy from reproduction to physical activity. Moderate exercise is healthy, but if you're exercising intensely and have missed 3+ periods, see a healthcare provider. Reducing intensity and ensuring adequate calorie intake usually helps.

question: Can illness delay my period
alternate_questions: Why did being sick delay my period
answer: Yes, illness can delay your period. When your body is fighting infection, it prioritizes immune function over reproduction. Fever, significant illness, or recovery from surgery can all disrupt your cycle. COVID-19 has been reported to cause cycle changes in some people. The delay is usually temporary, and your cycle should return to normal within 1-2 months after recovery.

question: Can medication delay my period
alternate_questions: Why did my medicine delay my period
answer: Yes, certain medications can delay your period. Common culprits include: emergency contraception, hormonal birth control changes, antidepressants (especially SSRIs), antipsychotics, thyroid medications, chemotherapy, and some herbal supplements. Antibiotics don't typically affect periods directly, but the illness they're treating might. If you started a new medication and your period is late, check the side effects or ask your prescribing doctor.

question: Can birth control delay my period
answer: Yes, starting, stopping, or changing birth control can delay your period. It takes time for your body to adjust to new hormone levels. Some methods like the hormonal IUD or implant can make periods very light or stop altogether, which is normal. Emergency contraception can delay your next period by up to a week. If you've missed pills, your period might be irregular. If concerned, take a pregnancy test and consult your provider.

question: Can breastfeeding delay my period
answer: Yes, breastfeeding commonly delays the return of your period. This is called lactational amenorrhea. Prolactin, the hormone that produces milk, suppresses ovulation. The more frequently you nurse, the more likely your period will stay away. This is nature's way of spacing pregnancies. However, you can still ovulate before your first postpartum period, so contraception is needed if you want to avoid pregnancy.

question: Can PCOS delay my period
answer: Yes, PCOS is a common cause of delayed or absent periods. In PCOS, hormonal imbalances (high androgens, irregular LH/FSH ratios) prevent regular ovulation. Without ovulation, there's no trigger for the luteal phase and subsequent period. Some people with PCOS have very irregular cycles, while others may go months without a period. If you suspect PCOS, look for other symptoms like acne, excess hair growth, and weight gain, and see a healthcare provider.

question: Can thyroid problems delay my period
answer: Yes, both underactive (hypothyroidism) and overactive (hyperthyroidism) thyroid can delay or disrupt your period. Thyroid hormones interact closely with reproductive hormones. Hypothyroidism often causes heavier, more frequent, or irregular periods, while hyperthyroidism may cause lighter or less frequent periods. A simple blood test (TSH, T3, T4) can check your thyroid function. Treatment usually restores normal cycles.

question: Can perimenopause delay my period
alternate_questions: Why are my periods getting further apart
answer: Yes, perimenopause (the transition to menopause, typically ages 40-55) commonly causes delayed or irregular periods. As ovarian function declines, ovulation becomes less predictable, leading to longer cycles, skipped periods, or changes in flow. This is a normal part of aging. However, any bleeding changes after 45 should be discussed with a doctor to rule out other conditions like fibroids or endometrial issues.

question: When should I take a pregnancy test
answer: Take a pregnancy test on the first day of your missed period for the most accurate result. Testing earlier may give a false negative because hCG levels aren't high enough yet. If your cycles are irregular, wait at least 21 days after unprotected sex. Use first morning urine for best results. If negative but your period still doesn't come, retest in 3-7 days. Blood tests at a doctor's office can detect pregnancy even earlier.

question: Can I delay my period on purpose
answer: Yes, you can delay your period using hormonal birth control. If you're on the combined pill, you can skip the placebo week and start the next pack immediately. Some doctors prescribe norethisterone (a progesterone pill) to delay periods for special events. These methods should be discussed with a healthcare provider first. Natural methods like stress management or extreme exercise are not recommended and can be harmful.

question: Why did my period come early after being late
alternate_questions: Why is my cycle so unpredictable
answer: Having a late period followed by an early one often indicates hormonal fluctuations, commonly caused by stress, lifestyle changes, or the aftermath of a previous cycle disruption. Your body may be trying to recalibrate. This pattern can also occur with perimenopause, thyroid issues, or PCOS. If this happens occasionally, it's usually not concerning. If it becomes a pattern over 3+ months, consult a healthcare provider.

question: Can emotional trauma delay my period
answer: Yes, significant emotional trauma, grief, or shock can delay or stop your period. The brain-ovary connection is sensitive to emotional states. Severe stress triggers cortisol release, which can suppress reproductive hormones. This is a protective mechanism. Your period usually returns once you've processed the trauma or as your emotional state stabilizes. If your period hasn't returned after 2-3 months, see a healthcare provider.

question: Can diet changes delay my period
answer: Yes, significant diet changes can delay your period. Very low-calorie diets, extreme fasting, or sudden elimination of food groups can cause nutritional deficiencies that affect hormones. Vegan diets may lack B12 and iron if not well-planned. Keto diets sometimes cause initial cycle disruption. Your body needs adequate calories, protein, and healthy fats to maintain regular cycles. Gradual dietary changes and proper nutrition help prevent delays.
